Permission
per-MISH-un
n. (leave granted; allowance as distinguished from command)
Greek suggnome, literally a thinking-with, a concession — agreement to allow rather than a requirement to obey. Latin permissio, from permittere, to let through, to let go.

Biblical Definition

But I speak this by permission, and not of commandment. Paul has just given his counsel about abstinence within marriage, and he pauses to mark the status of what he has said. The distinction is between a concession and a command. What he has allowed — a season of abstinence by mutual consent for prayer — is permitted, not required; a Christian couple who never take such a season have disobeyed nothing. The verse is therefore a small model of a large habit: the apostle is careful to tell his readers how binding each thing he says is. In the same chapter he distinguishes what he has from the Lord, what he says of himself, and what is concession, and he expects the church to weigh the difference. This is not uncertainty about his authority. Paul elsewhere writes with full apostolic weight and expects obedience. It is precision about the kind of thing being said, and it guards the conscience in both directions. Where God has commanded, no man may loosen; where God has permitted, no man may bind. Paul immediately adds the reason such matters cannot be legislated uniformly: every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): the act of permitting or allowing; leave; license or liberty granted; allowance, as distinguished from command.

expand to see more

PERMISSION, n. The act of permitting or allowing.

PERMISSION, n. Allowance; license or liberty granted; leave.

PERMIT, v.t. To allow; to grant leave or liberty to by express consent.

COMMANDMENT, n. A command; a mandate; an order or injunction given by authority.

CONCESSION, n. The act of granting or yielding, usually implying a demand, claim or request from the party to whom it is made.

Key Scripture

1 Corinthians 7:6 — "But I speak this by permission, and not of commandment."

1 Corinthians 7:7 — "For I would that all men were even as I myself. But every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that."

1 Corinthians 7:5 — "Defraud ye not one the other, except it be with consent for a time, that ye may give yourselves to fasting and prayer; and come together again, that Satan tempt you not for your incontinency."

1 Corinthians 7:2 — "Nevertheless, to avoid fornication, let every man have his own wife, and let every woman have her own husband."

Modern Corruption

The verse is used to make Paul's teaching generally optional, as though he were offering opinions; he is doing the opposite, marking precisely which of his words bind and which do not.

expand to see more

A common use of 1 Corinthians 7:6 is to relativise apostolic teaching as such: if Paul concedes that he sometimes speaks by permission, then his instructions may be weighed as personal counsel wherever a reader finds them inconvenient. The inference runs backward. A writer who carefully labels one sentence as concession is telling you that the unlabelled sentences are not. Paul does exactly the same within this chapter, distinguishing what he has of the Lord from what he says himself, and the distinction only means anything because his ordinary word carries authority. Scripture is God-breathed throughout, and its own internal markers of command and concession are part of what is breathed out.

The opposite error binds where God has left free. A church that turns Paul's concession into a requirement — mandating seasons of abstinence, or ranking those who practise them — has done to this verse what Rome did to celibacy at large, and it burdens consciences God has not burdened. The doctrine of Christian liberty rests on the difference this verse marks. Where Scripture commands, the conscience is bound absolutely; where Scripture permits, no church, elder, or movement may bind it, and the attempt is itself a fault.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek suggnome (G4774), a concession or allowance; epitage (G2003), an injunction or command; charisma (G5486), a gift of grace.

expand to see more

Greek suggnome (G4774) — concession, allowance; rendered permission, its only occurrence.

Greek epitage (G2003) — an injunction, a command; the term Paul expressly denies of this counsel.

Greek charisma (G5486) — a gift of grace; rendered proper gift, the reason such matters differ between believers.

Greek epitasso (G2004) — to enjoin, to order; the verb behind commandment.

Greek eleutheria (G1657) — liberty; the doctrine that rests on the distinction this verse draws.

Usage

"“by permission, and not of commandment” — the status of the counsel, marked by the apostle."

"“every man hath his proper gift of God” — why such matters are not legislated uniformly."

"“except it be with consent for a time” — the concession itself."
